overviewHtml:
This graded quiz assesses your understanding of Merleau-Ponty's accounts of others, language, and art, and their extension in critical phenomenology. You'll be asked about intercorporeality, speech as gesture, painting and vision, and critical phenomenology.

Note: Aim for a score of 80 percent or higher. If you score lower, use the feedback to review the topics you missed, then retake the quiz.

forms.stemHtml: Why does Merleau-Ponty say a village or a path makes others present to you?

options.html: Because you infer each builder's mind by analogy with yours
options.text: Because you infer each builder's mind by analogy with yours
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on cultural objects and the argument from analogy.

options.html: Because cultural objects bear the traces of human purposes
options.text: Because cultural objects bear the traces of human purposes
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Others are present in them as an anonymous "someone," before any particular person appears.

options.html: Because you remember the particular people who built them
options.text: Because you remember the particular people who built them
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on cultural objects and the argument from analogy.

options.html: Because paths are physical causes of social behavior
options.text: Because paths are physical causes of social behavior
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on cultural objects and the argument from analogy.

forms.stemHtml: How does Merleau-Ponty's intercorporeality differ from Sartre's account of the look?

options.html: Intercorporeality makes the other an object, while the look does not
options.text: Intercorporeality makes the other an object, while the look does not
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading comparing intercorporeality with pairing and the look.

options.html: The look makes me an object, while coupling is mutual
options.text: The look makes me an object, while coupling is mutual
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For Sartre, the other's look objectifies me. For Merleau-Ponty, two body-subjects respond to each other.

options.html: Both describe the same relation in different words
options.text: Both describe the same relation in different words
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading comparing intercorporeality with pairing and the look.

options.html: The look is bodily, while intercorporeality is purely mental
options.text: The look is bodily, while intercorporeality is purely mental
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading comparing intercorporeality with pairing and the look.

forms.stemHtml: What is Merleau-Ponty's term for the direct, bodily attunement of two body-subjects, in which each responds to the other's conduct as meaningful, without inference? Enter one word.

options.html: coupling
options.text: coupling
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Coupling is the relation that intercorporeality names.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on bodily coupling, intercorporeality, and the limits of access to others.

forms.stemHtml: According to the translation model of speech, what is speaking?

options.html: Encoding a thought that is already complete into words
options.text: Encoding a thought that is already complete into words
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is the model Merleau-Ponty rejects: for him, speech accomplishes thought.

options.html: Completing a thought in the act of expressing it
options.text: Completing a thought in the act of expressing it
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on translation models and the gestural account of language.

options.html: Producing sounds with no meaning at all
options.text: Producing sounds with no meaning at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on translation models and the gestural account of language.

options.html: Creating new meaning from sedimented language
options.text: Creating new meaning from sedimented language
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on translation models and the gestural account of language.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are examples of spoken speech, in Merleau-Ponty's sense? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: A greeting used without thinking about its words
options.text: A greeting used without thinking about its words
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! It draws on sedimented, available language.

options.html: A familiar technical term used in its standard sense
options.text: A familiar technical term used in its standard sense
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! It's part of a shared stock of words and meanings.

options.html: A common idiom used in everyday conversation
options.text: A common idiom used in everyday conversation
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! It's available language used without effort.

options.html: A poet's metaphor that has never been used before
options.text: A poet's metaphor that has never been used before
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on speaking speech, spoken speech, and sedimentation.

options.html: A scientist's new concept for an unexpected finding
options.text: A scientist's new concept for an unexpected finding
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on speaking speech, spoken speech, and sedimentation.

forms.stemHtml: What is the term for the perspective of perception as lived by a moving, embodied perceiver, in which things appear with the deformations of an unfolding view? Enter two words.

options.html: lived perspective
options.text: lived perspective
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Merleau-Ponty argues that Cézanne's "distortions" follow lived perspective.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Cézanne's project and lived perspective.

forms.stemHtml: Why does Descartes, in the Optics, use copperplate engravings to explain vision?

options.html: Because engravings resemble their objects more closely than paintings
options.text: Because engravings resemble their objects more closely than paintings
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on "Eye and Mind" and Descartes's Optics.

options.html: Because they represent things well without resembling them
options.text: Because they represent things well without resembling them
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! On this model, seeing is the mind reading signs that needn't resemble their objects.

options.html: Because engravings capture color and depth
options.text: Because engravings capture color and depth
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on "Eye and Mind" and Descartes's Optics.

options.html: Because Descartes was himself an engraver
options.text: Because Descartes was himself an engraver
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on "Eye and Mind" and Descartes's Optics.

forms.stemHtml: What happens to the body schema in the street encounter Fanon describes?

options.html: It is strengthened by the encounter
options.text: It is strengthened by the encounter
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Fanon's historico-racial and epidermal racial schemas.

options.html: It collapses, displaced by an epidermal racial schema
options.text: It collapses, displaced by an epidermal racial schema
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Fixed by a racializing look, Fanon lives his body as its skin color seen by others.

options.html: It is unaffected, since it is purely physiological
options.text: It is unaffected, since it is purely physiological
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Fanon's historico-racial and epidermal racial schemas.

options.html: It is replaced by a conscious theory of race
options.text: It is replaced by a conscious theory of race
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Fanon's historico-racial and epidermal racial schemas.

forms.stemHtml: How does Young explain the modalities of feminine motility she describes?

options.html: By a biological "feminine attitude," as Straus did
options.text: By a biological "feminine attitude," as Straus did
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Young's phenomenology of feminine motility.

options.html: By social situation: training, practice, and being looked at
options.text: By social situation: training, practice, and being looked at
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Young rejects biological explanation and traces the modalities to situation.

options.html: By individual choices that each woman could simply reverse
options.text: By individual choices that each woman could simply reverse
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Young's phenomenology of feminine motility.

options.html: By differences in the body schema present at birth
options.text: By differences in the body schema present at birth
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Young's phenomenology of feminine motility.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are claims Ahmed makes about lines? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Lines are made by being followed
options.text: Lines are made by being followed
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Each time a body follows a line, the line becomes clearer.

options.html: Bodies take shape by following lines
options.text: Bodies take shape by following lines
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Following lines gives bodies their habits and tendencies.

options.html: Heterosexuality can function as a straight line
options.text: Heterosexuality can function as a straight line
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! It's a path many bodies are expected to follow.

options.html: Lines are fixed by nature and can't change
options.text: Lines are fixed by nature and can't change
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Ahmed's orientation, lines, and disorientation.

options.html: Following a line has no effect on what is within reach
options.text: Following a line has no effect on what is within reach
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Ahmed's orientation, lines, and disorientation.

forms.stemHtml: What does the argument from analogy claim about how we know other minds?

options.html: That we perceive other minds directly in bodily conduct
options.text: That we perceive other minds directly in bodily conduct
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on cultural objects and the argument from analogy.

options.html: That other minds can never be known in any way
options.text: That other minds can never be known in any way
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on cultural objects and the argument from analogy.

options.html: That we infer them from bodies that behave as ours does
options.text: That we infer them from bodies that behave as ours does
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Because another body behaves as mine does, I infer it's animated by a mind like mine.

options.html: That minds are shared among all members of a culture
options.text: That minds are shared among all members of a culture
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on cultural objects and the argument from analogy.

forms.stemHtml: What does Gallagher's interaction theory claim about social understanding?

options.html: That we understand others mainly by theorizing about their beliefs
options.text: That we understand others mainly by theorizing about their beliefs
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on interaction theory and the evidence disputes.

options.html: That we understand others by simulating their minds with ours
options.text: That we understand others by simulating their minds with ours
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on interaction theory and the evidence disputes.

options.html: That it's achieved mainly through embodied interaction
options.text: That it's achieved mainly through embodied interaction
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Interaction theory stresses direct perception of intentions and emotions in interaction.

options.html: That social understanding is impossible without language
options.text: That social understanding is impossible without language
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on interaction theory and the evidence disputes.

forms.stemHtml: What is Merleau-Ponty's term for the irreducible fact that each person lives their own experience, so that the other's experience, as they live it, is never fully mine? Enter two words.

options.html: lived solitude
options.text: lived solitude
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Direct perception of others doesn't give full access to their experience.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on bodily coupling, intercorporeality, and the limits of access to others.

forms.stemHtml: Merleau-Ponty rejects two classical accounts of language. What does the intellectualist account hold?

options.html: That words are reflexes triggered by stimuli
options.text: That words are reflexes triggered by stimuli
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on speech accomplishing thought and the word as gesture.

options.html: That words are signs of already finished thoughts
options.text: That words are signs of already finished thoughts
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! On this account the word adds nothing. Merleau-Ponty argues it accomplishes the thought.

options.html: That words are gestures that complete thought
options.text: That words are gestures that complete thought
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on speech accomplishing thought and the word as gesture.

options.html: That words have no relation to thought
options.text: That words have no relation to thought
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on speech accomplishing thought and the word as gesture.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following does Merleau-Ponty's gestural account of language hold? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: A word's meaning is in the expressive act itself
options.text: A word's meaning is in the expressive act itself
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! As anger is in an angry gesture, meaning is in the word as spoken.

options.html: New meanings can arise in language
options.text: New meanings can arise in language
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Speaking speech brings new meaning into being.

options.html: We never think without speaking aloud
options.text: We never think without speaking aloud
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on translation models and the gestural account of language.

options.html: Words are labels for finished thoughts
options.text: Words are labels for finished thoughts
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on translation models and the gestural account of language.

forms.stemHtml: What is Merleau-Ponty's term, in the Cézanne essay, for perception as it is lived before it settles into determinate objects and the distinctions of thought? Enter two words.

options.html: primordial perception
options.text: primordial perception
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is what Cézanne tried to paint, on Merleau-Ponty's reading.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Cézanne's project and lived perspective.

forms.stemHtml: How does Merleau-Ponty's account of depth in "Eye and Mind" differ from Descartes's?

options.html: Both treat depth as a third dimension derived from height and width
options.text: Both treat depth as a third dimension derived from height and width
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on "Eye and Mind" and Descartes's Optics.

options.html: Merleau-Ponty treats depth as an illusion of painting
options.text: Merleau-Ponty treats depth as an illusion of painting
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on "Eye and Mind" and Descartes's Optics.

options.html: He treats it as things enveloping one another, lived first
options.text: He treats it as things enveloping one another, lived first
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For Descartes, depth is derived. For Merleau-Ponty, it's lived by a body among things before it's measured.

options.html: Descartes treats depth as lived, Merleau-Ponty as measured
options.text: Descartes treats depth as lived, Merleau-Ponty as measured
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on "Eye and Mind" and Descartes's Optics.

forms.stemHtml: What does Fanon mean when he says he is "overdetermined from without"?

options.html: He is defined in advance by others' images of how he looks
options.text: He is defined in advance by others' images of how he looks
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! His appearance is taken to reveal what he is, before he can act.

options.html: He is caused to act by physical forces outside his body
options.text: He is caused to act by physical forces outside his body
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Fanon's historico-racial and epidermal racial schemas.

options.html: He has too many possible actions to choose among
options.text: He has too many possible actions to choose among
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Fanon's historico-racial and epidermal racial schemas.

options.html: He is unaware of how others see him
options.text: He is unaware of how others see him
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Fanon's historico-racial and epidermal racial schemas.

forms.stemHtml: In throwing a ball, a person moves only the arm while the rest of the body stays still. Which of Young's modalities does this illustrate?

options.html: Ambiguous transcendence
options.text: Ambiguous transcendence
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Young's phenomenology of feminine motility.

options.html: Inhibited intentionality
options.text: Inhibited intentionality
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Young's phenomenology of feminine motility.

options.html: Discontinuous unity
options.text: Discontinuous unity
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Some parts of the body move while others stay inert, splitting the body's unity in action.

options.html: Epidermal racial schema
options.text: Epidermal racial schema
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Young's phenomenology of feminine motility.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following describe quasi-transcendental structures, as critical phenomenology uses the term? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: They are contingent and historical
options.text: They are contingent and historical
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! They could be otherwise, which is why they're only "quasi"-transcendental.

options.html: They shape experience as deeply as its conditions
options.text: They shape experience as deeply as its conditions
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For those who live within them, they structure perception and action from the start.

options.html: They are conditions of all possible experience
options.text: They are conditions of all possible experience
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on critical phenomenology and its debates.

options.html: They exist only as ideas in individual minds
options.text: They exist only as ideas in individual minds
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on critical phenomenology and its debates.

forms.stemHtml: What does Merleau-Ponty mean by the human world?

options.html: The sum of all the individual minds that exist
options.text: The sum of all the individual minds that exist
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on cultural objects and the argument from analogy.

options.html: The world as physics describes it, without meaning
options.text: The world as physics describes it, without meaning
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on cultural objects and the argument from analogy.

options.html: The world shaped by human action, where others are present
options.text: The world shaped by human action, where others are present
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! In the human world, others are always already present, for example in cultural objects.

options.html: A private world that each person constructs alone
options.text: A private world that each person constructs alone
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on cultural objects and the argument from analogy.

options.html: It was never reported in the research literature
options.text: It was never reported in the research literature

forms.stemHtml: What is Husserl's term, translated from Paarung, for the passive, associative linking in which another body similar to one's own is apprehended as a lived body too? Enter one word.

options.html: pairing
options.text: pairing
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Merleau-Ponty's intercorporeality is often compared with Husserl's pairing.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading comparing intercorporeality with pairing and the look.

forms.stemHtml: How does Merleau-Ponty describe sexuality, in its relation to a person's life?

options.html: As a drive confined to one bodily function
options.text: As a drive confined to one bodily function

options.html: As a set of ideas held in consciousness
options.text: As a set of ideas held in consciousness
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on sexuality and the expressive body.

options.html: As an atmosphere diffused through a whole life

options.html: As a symptom to be explained by early memories
options.text: As a symptom to be explained by early memories

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are true of sedimentation, in Merleau-Ponty's account? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: It turns new expression into available language
options.text: It turns new expression into available language
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Acts of expression settle into shared meanings.

options.html: It lets later speakers use meanings without re-creating them
options.text: It lets later speakers use meanings without re-creating them
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! That's what makes spoken speech available.

options.html: It connects speaking speech with spoken speech
options.text: It connects speaking speech with spoken speech
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Today's speaking speech can become tomorrow's spoken speech.

options.html: It makes all later expression unnecessary
options.text: It makes all later expression unnecessary
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on speaking speech, spoken speech, and sedimentation.

options.html: It happens only in written language
options.text: It happens only in written language
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on speaking speech, spoken speech, and sedimentation.

forms.stemHtml: What is Merleau-Ponty's term for the way language and painting signify through the relations among their elements, rather than by pointing directly to a meaning set out in advance? Enter two words.

options.html: indirect language
options.text: indirect language
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Merleau-Ponty calls painting a tacit language for this reason.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on "Indirect Language," painting, and style.

forms.stemHtml: How does Merleau-Ponty treat the relation between Cézanne's life and his work?

options.text: The work is fully explained by Cézanne's temperament

options.html: The life and work have nothing to do with each other

options.html: They communicate: the work gives the life its meaning

options.html: The life is a symptom that the work conceals

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following accurately describe the debate over critical phenomenology's relation to classical phenomenology? (Select all that apply.)
